title: Occlusion & the bite
blurb: How the teeth meet: centric occlusion, overjet and overbite, the incisor classes, and checking the bite chairside.
question: At an orthodontic assessment for a 12-year-old, the dentist says: 'Class II division 1, overjet 9 mm, overbite increased.' You are recording the findings. What does each part mean, and how would the child's front teeth look?

teach.body: Occlusion is the way the upper and lower teeth meet when the jaws close. In a normal bite the upper arch is slightly larger than the lower, so the upper front teeth overlap the lowers at the front and the upper back teeth sit just outside the lowers. Most teeth bite against two opposing teeth. When the teeth meet in a poor relationship, it is called a malocclusion: crowding, spacing, crossbites, open bites and jaw imbalances are all examples.

Centric occlusion (also called the intercuspal position) is when the teeth are fully meshed together, with the most contact between the cusps. It depends on the teeth. Centric relation is a jaw position: the condyles are seated in their sockets, whatever the teeth are doing. Because it can be repeated reliably even without teeth, it is used when recording the bite for complete dentures. At rest, the teeth are slightly apart: this gap is the freeway space, usually about 2–4 mm.

rows.label: Measured
values: Upper incisal edge to lower labial surface
How far uppers cover the lowers

rows.label: Normal
values: About a third of the lower incisor

teach.caption: An open bite means no vertical overlap: the front teeth don't meet when the back teeth are together. A persistent thumb-sucking habit is a common cause.
A large overjet also leaves the upper incisors more exposed to injury in a fall.

teach.body: UK orthodontists classify the bite by where the lower incisor edges meet the upper incisors. The reference point is the cingulum plateau: the bump on the palatal surface of the upper incisor near the gum. In Class I the lower incisors bite on or just below it. In Class II they sit behind it. In Class III they sit in front of it. Class II is split by the angle of the upper central incisors.

root.label: Lower incisor edge vs upper cingulum

children.label: Class I
children.sub: On or just below it. Normal overjet

children.label: Class III
children.sub: In front of it. Overjet reduced or reversed

teach.caption: Proclined = tipped forwards. Retroclined = tipped backwards.

teach.h: The teeth used to describe the bite
teach.caption: Incisors give the incisor class, overjet and overbite. First molars give the molar relationship: in Class I the mesiobuccal cusp of the upper 6 sits in the buccal groove of the lower 6.

teach.body: After a filling or crown, the dentist checks for a high spot. You hand over articulating paper in Miller's forceps; the patient taps and grinds, and coloured marks show where the teeth hit. A high restoration can cause pain on biting and can fracture. For crowns, bridges and dentures you may mix a bite registration material (wax or silicone) to record how the teeth meet. If a patient says a new filling 'feels high', always tell the dentist before they leave.

teach.text: Overjet is HORIZONTAL (think jet flying forwards). Overbite is VERTICAL (think bite down). Class II div 1 = big overjet with uppers sticking out; Class II div 2 = uppers tipped back with a deep overbite.

items: Centric occlusion: teeth fully meshed. Centric relation: condyles seated, used for denture bite records.
Overjet: horizontal, normal about 2–4 mm. Overbite: vertical, normal about a third of the lower incisor.
Class I on the cingulum, Class II behind it (div 1 proclined, div 2 retroclined), Class III in front.
Articulating paper in Miller's forceps shows high spots; report any 'high' filling to the dentist.

summary: You can now define occlusion, centric occlusion, centric relation and freeway space, tell overjet from overbite and give their normal values, classify incisor relationships as Class I, II (division 1 or 2) or III, and explain how the bite is checked and recorded chairside.

options: The vertical overlap of the incisors
The horizontal overlap of the incisors
The gap between the teeth with the jaw at rest
The contact of the back teeth
A.why: Overjet is the horizontal distance from the upper incisal edge to the labial surface of the lower incisor.

whyNot.2: The gap between the teeth at rest is the freeway space.
whyNot.3: Back-teeth contact describes the buccal segment relationship, not the overjet.

A.q: A patient's lower incisor edges bite in front of the cingulum plateau of the upper incisors. Which incisor class is this?
A.why: In Class III the lower incisor edges lie in front of the upper cingulum plateau, so the overjet is reduced or reversed.

whyNot.0: In Class I the lower incisors bite on or just below the cingulum plateau.
whyNot.1: In Class II the lower incisors sit behind the cingulum plateau.
whyNot.2: Class II division 2 also has the lower incisors behind the cingulum plateau.

A.q: Just after a new amalgam, the patient says the tooth feels high when they bite. What should the dental nurse do?
options: Tell them it will settle in a week
Book a review appointment in six months
Smooth the filling with a bur
Ask the dentist to check the occlusion
A.why: A high restoration can cause pain and fracture, so the dentist must check and adjust it before the patient leaves.

whyNot.0: A high filling won't reliably settle and can cause pain or fracture.
whyNot.1: Waiting six months leaves the problem untreated.
whyNot.2: Adjusting a restoration is the dentist's task, not the nurse's.

B.q: Which describes a Class II division 2 incisor relationship?
options: Upper centrals retroclined with a deep overbite
Upper incisors proclined with a large overjet
Lower incisors biting in front of the uppers
Lower incisors resting on the upper cingulum plateau
B.why: In Class II division 2 the upper central incisors are tipped back (retroclined) and the overbite is usually deep.

whyNot.1: Proclined uppers with a large overjet describe Class II division 1.
whyNot.2: Lowers in front of the uppers describe Class III.
whyNot.3: Lowers biting on the cingulum plateau describe Class I.

B.q: What is the normal overjet in an adult?
B.why: A normal overjet is about 2–4 mm.

whyNot.0: An overjet of 0 mm means edge-to-edge incisors, which is reduced.
whyNot.2: 6–8 mm is increased, as seen in Class II division 1.
whyNot.3: 10 mm is a markedly increased overjet.

B.q: Which instrument holds articulating paper while the dentist checks a patient's bite?
B.why: Miller's forceps are designed to grip articulating paper so the patient can bite on it.

whyNot.0: College tweezers carry small items such as cotton pellets.
whyNot.1: Mosquito forceps are small artery forceps used in surgery.
whyNot.3: A flat plastic places and shapes restorative materials.

C.q: Which term describes the position where the upper and lower teeth fit together with maximum contact?
C.why: Centric occlusion (the intercuspal position) is when the teeth are fully meshed with the most cusp contact.

whyNot.1: Freeway space is the small gap between the teeth when the jaw is at rest.
whyNot.2: Protrusive occlusion is with the mandible moved forwards, so the cusps are not fully meshed.
whyNot.3: In the rest position the teeth are apart, not in contact.

C.q: A child's front teeth do not meet at all when their back teeth are together. What is this called?
C.why: An anterior open bite means there is no vertical overlap of the incisors when the back teeth meet.

whyNot.0: A deep overbite is too much vertical overlap, the opposite.
whyNot.1: A reversed overjet means the lowers are in front of the uppers.
whyNot.2: A posterior crossbite involves back teeth meeting the wrong way side to side.

C.q: Why is centric relation used when recording the bite for complete dentures?
options: It depends on the cusps of the teeth
It is the widest the jaw can open
It is a repeatable jaw position
C.why: Centric relation is set by the condyles seated in their sockets, so it can be repeated even when there are no teeth.

whyNot.0: Centric occlusion depends on the teeth; centric relation does not.
whyNot.1: Centric relation is a closed jaw position, not maximum opening.
whyNot.3: Dentures must keep a freeway space; centric relation doesn't remove it.

reteach.title: Look at the front teeth from the side
reteach.question: Imagine looking at someone's front teeth side-on while they bite together. What two measurements can you see, and what does the class tell you?

blocks.body: From the side, the upper front teeth normally sit a little in front of the lowers, like a lid that overhangs a box. How far the lid sticks out forwards is the overjet. How far the lid comes down over the box is the overbite. If the lid sticks out a long way, the lowers are too far back: Class II. If the box is in front of the lid, the lowers are too far forward: Class III. A lid that fits neatly is Class I.

blocks.h: The three classes in a sentence

blocks.text: JET goes FORWARDS (horizontal). BITE comes DOWN (vertical).

explain.h: Centric occlusion, centric relation, freeway space
explain.body: Centric occlusion: teeth fully meshed. Centric relation: condyles seated in the fossae, independent of the teeth and repeatable. Freeway space: the 2–4 mm gap between the teeth when the jaw is relaxed at rest.

options: The gap between teeth at rest
The space left after an extraction
The gap between two crowded teeth
test.why: Freeway space is the small gap, usually about 2–4 mm, between the upper and lower teeth when the jaw is at rest.

whyNot.1: Space after an extraction is simply an edentulous space.
whyNot.2: Overlap of the incisors is the overjet and overbite.
whyNot.3: Crowded teeth have too little space, not a freeway space.

explain.body: Overjet is horizontal: from the upper incisal edge to the front of the lower incisor, normally about 2–4 mm. Overbite is vertical: how far the upper incisors cover the lowers, normally about a third of the lower incisor crown.

test.q: The dentist says a patient has a 'deep bite'. Which measurement is increased?
test.why: A deep bite means the upper incisors cover the lowers more than normal: an increased overbite.

whyNot.1: Freeway space is the gap at rest, not the incisor overlap.
whyNot.3: Arch width is not what 'deep bite' describes.

explain.body: Measured against the upper cingulum plateau. Class I: lowers on or just below it. Class II: lowers behind it (div 1 proclined uppers and big overjet; div 2 retroclined upper centrals and deep overbite). Class III: lowers in front of it.

items.label: in front of it: reduced or reversed overjet

test.q: A child's upper incisors stick out with an overjet of 8 mm. Which class is most likely?
test.why: Proclined upper incisors with an increased overjet are typical of Class II division 1.

whyNot.0: Class I has a normal overjet.
whyNot.1: Class III has a reduced or reversed overjet.
whyNot.2: Class II division 2 has retroclined upper centrals, usually with a small overjet.

explain.body: Articulating paper in Miller's forceps marks where teeth hit, so the dentist can adjust high spots. Bite registration material records how the jaws meet for crowns, bridges and dentures. Report any 'high' feeling straight away.

test.q: What is articulating paper used for?
test.why: Articulating paper leaves coloured marks where the teeth contact, showing any high spots.

whyNot.0: Composites are polished with discs, strips or polishing points.
whyNot.2: A full bite registration uses wax or silicone.
whyNot.3: Teeth are separated with wedges or separators.
